definition: Amplify means to increase the strength or intensity of something.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word amplify. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know amplify should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Cupping his hands into a cone, the lifeguard amplified his shout enough to reach the swimmers at the far buoy.
A snack boosts your energy for an hour; amplify goes further, markedly strengthening a sound or feeling rather than giving it a small push.
Supercharge sits past amplify on the dial: amplifying strengthens the engine's note, while supercharging forces the engine itself past its everyday limits.

Augment means to make something larger by adding more to it — new lanes added to a highway, fresh voices added to a choir. Amplify adds nothing new; it takes what is already there and turns its strength up. Augmenting brings new material; amplifying strengthens the existing signal.

Strengthen means to make something sturdier or more solid — a bridge, a friendship, an argument braced against attack. Amplify strengthens in one particular direction: it turns up the intensity of a sound, a signal, or a feeling so it registers more forcefully, not so it holds together better.

Amplify is the precise verb because something that already existed was made stronger.
The espressos invented nothing; they took an existing signal — her nerves — and turned it up.
That is amplify's home ground: strengthening what is already present, whether a sound, a signal, or a feeling.
Amplify strengthens what already exists — a sound, a signal, a feeling.

Its unit-mates divide the work: intensify says the degree itself climbs (heat, pressure, a rivalry); magnify makes a thing merely look bigger or weightier than it is; inflate pushes a figure or claim past its true amount.
Reach for amplify when something real gets turned up, most naturally a sound or an emotion.

The valley's one radio mast sits on Copper Ridge, and everything the station sends must first climb there by cable.
In the ridge hut, a bank of equipment takes the studio's faint signal and sets about amplifying it several thousandfold before the antenna lets it go.
Nothing about the broadcast changes on the ridge — no new songs, no added voices.
The same program simply leaves the hilltop strong enough to cross forty miles of ranchland.
Old-timers remember when the hut burned and the station kept sending anyway: the studio feed still worked, but no receiver past the town line could catch the whisper.
The engineer likes to put it plainly: the ridge does not make the show better.
